**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Thursday

---

We've reached the point in the quarter where the queue for our inference cluster is long enough that people are asking, reasonably, whether we should just buy more hardware. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this before we commit either way, because I believe the framing matters more than the answer, and the answer is less obvious than the queue length suggests.

The case for buying is straightforward. Our p95 latency on batch jobs has crept from forty minutes to nearly three hours over the past two months, and interactive users are now seeing queue waits that make experimentation genuinely unpleasant. Every week of degraded latency has a real cost, not just in frustration but in the experiments people quietly decide not to run. That's the opportunity cost that never shows up in a dashboard: the fine-tuning run someone skipped, the eval sweep that got cut in half. If we treat those as lost, the marginal GPU pays for itself quickly. Hardware is also an asset we understand how to buy. Procurement knows the process, the vendor relationship exists, and a purchase order is a decision we can make on Monday and stop thinking about.

But I want to push back on the instinct, including my own, that more capacity is automatically the right response. Our utilisation numbers tell a more complicated story. Average utilisation across the cluster sits around 55%, which means nearly half of what we pay for in power, cooling, and depreciation is idle at any given moment. The problem is less that we lack capacity and more that our capacity is badly shaped: long-running batch jobs monopolise cards overnight while the interactive queue sits empty, then the pattern inverts during the day. A modest investment in scheduling — better partitioning between batch and interactive workloads, checkpoint-and-preempt for long jobs, and honestly just asking people to tag their workloads properly — could plausibly recover 20 to 30 percentage points of effective utilisation. That is the equivalent of several new cards for the price of a few engineering weeks, and unlike a purchase order, that engineering work compounds: the scheduler improvements carry forward to whatever hardware we own, forever.

There's also the reliability angle, which cuts both ways. More hardware means more physical surface area for failure — more cards to fail, more nodes to drift, more maintenance windows — and our current monitoring is not good enough that I'd trust us to operate a cluster twice this size without incident. Conversely, improving utilisation through preemption and checkpointing introduces its own failure modes: a badly implemented preemption policy can lose someone's twelve-hour training run, which would cost us more goodwill than the queue ever did. Either path carries execution risk; neither is free.

On reversibility, the asymmetry favours the software route. If we buy four more nodes and the demand turns out to be a two-month spike from a project that ships or dies, we're holding depreciating hardware and paying for power on idle silicon. If we invest in scheduling and the demand is real and sustained, we've lost a few weeks and gained permanent tooling — and we can still buy the hardware afterwards, better informed about what we actually need. Buying is a one-way door taken under uncertainty; scheduling work is a two-way door. When the doors differ like that, walk through the reversible one first.

So my recommendation is this: we spend the next four to six weeks on utilisation work — scheduling, partitioning, checkpointing, and honest instrumentation of who is using what — and we defer the purchase decision until we can see demand through a properly utilised cluster. I want to be clear about the uncertainty here. I can't promise scheduling recovers enough capacity to make buying unnecessary; if the demand growth is real and structural, we will still need hardware, and we'll have lost some calendar time by waiting. I think that risk is acceptable because the alternative is buying under a distorted signal, where queue length reflects our inefficiency as much as our demand, and we'd likely overbuy. The one commitment I'll make now: if utilisation work stalls or the interactive queue degrades further past a two-hour p95, we escalate the purchase immediately rather than letting the team suffer while we optimise.

Let's discuss at Monday's planning session.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure team
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've been asked to decide between two paths: purchasing additional local GPU hardware to expand our inference capacity, or investing engineering time to improve utilisation of the hardware we already own. I want to lay out the reasoning behind my recommendation, because the obvious answer — buy more — is, I believe, the wrong one right now, though not for the reasons people usually give.

First, the cost picture. The capital quote we received for two additional A100-class nodes comes to roughly $180,000, plus an estimated $2,400/month in power, cooling, and colocation. That is not an exorbitant sum by enterprise standards, but it is large relative to our team's size and budget, and it is largely irreversible. Once purchased, that hardware sits on our balance sheet, depreciates on a three-to-five-year schedule, and cannot easily be converted back into engineering headcount or other priorities if our needs change. Hardware purchases are, in practice, one-way doors. Improving utilisation, by contrast, is mostly a labour cost — perhaps six to eight weeks of focused work from two engineers — and it is almost entirely reversible. If our batching and scheduling improvements turn out not to help, we've lost some time and learned something concrete about our workload; we can then make the purchase decision with better information.

Second, utilisation itself. Our monitoring tells an uncomfortable story: our current fleet averages 31% GPU utilisation over a 24-hour cycle, with peaks near 85% during business hours and long troughs overnight. The problem is not that we lack compute; it's that our serving stack handles bursts poorly. Requests arrive individually, get processed individually, and the GPU spends much of its time on memory transfers and kernel launch overhead rather than actual computation. Standard techniques — continuous batching, better request coalescing, quantised model variants for latency-tolerant traffic, and time-shifting our batch evaluation jobs into the overnight trough — are well understood and, in comparable setups, have yielded two to threefold throughput improvements. If we achieve even a doubling, our effective capacity exceeds what the new hardware would provide, at a fraction of the cost.

Third, latency. This is the strongest argument for buying hardware, and I want to take it seriously. Adding capacity does reduce queueing latency under peak load, and some of our internal customers have complained about p99 response times during the afternoon crunch. But queueing latency under bursty load is precisely the problem that better batching and admission control solve most directly. Buying more machines without fixing the serving stack would likely reproduce the same inefficiency at larger scale — we would own more idle capacity during troughs and still see tail latency spikes during peaks, because the root cause is scheduling, not raw throughput. There is a risk that some latency gains from batching come at the cost of individual request latency (batched requests wait for batch-mates), so we should set an explicit p99 guardrail and fall back to smaller batch windows for latency-sensitive endpoints.

Fourth, reliability and opportunity cost. More hardware means more failure surface: more nodes to monitor, more drivers and firmware to patch, more thermal and power dependencies. Our on-call rotation is already thin. Meanwhile, the engineering time for the utilisation work is not free — it competes with the feature work the platform team has queued. But that trade is favourable: the utilisation improvements compound (they benefit every model we serve, now and in the future), whereas additional hardware only shifts a ceiling that we are nowhere near hitting.

My recommendation, then: defer the purchase for one quarter. Spend the next six weeks on the serving-stack improvements, with a clear success criterion — sustained utilisation above 60% and p99 latency under our agreed threshold at current peak load. If we hit those targets, we likely defer or cancel the purchase entirely. If we fall short, we will have a much sharper understanding of exactly what capacity we need, and the purchase case will write itself with real numbers behind it.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. Utilisation improvements sometimes look better in spreadsheets than in production, and our workload mix could shift in ways that make peak capacity genuinely binding. If a major internal customer commits to a large new workload next quarter, the calculus changes and we should revisit this immediately. But on the evidence we have today, the reversible, cheaper, higher-learning option is also the one most likely to solve the actual problem. We should take it.

Happy to discuss at Thursday's planning session.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Friday planning session

We've reached the point in our capacity planning where the honest question is no longer "do we need more compute?" but "do we need more compute, or do we need to stop wasting the compute we already pay for?" I want to lay out how I'm thinking about that trade before we commit budget, because the two paths have very different cost structures, risk profiles, and escape hatches.

Start with the obvious case for buying. Our queue times during the afternoon training window have crept from minutes to over an hour, and that latency is not free. Every hour a model sits in the queue is an hour an engineer waits, an experiment delayed, and a decision deferred. When I price that out — roughly six engineers whose iteration speed is gated on GPU availability — the implied cost of congestion is comparable to the amortised monthly cost of another node. On paper, buying looks justified. But that paper calculation assumes the congestion is real demand, and I'm increasingly unsure it is.

The utilisation data tells a messier story. Our fleet averages around 45% GPU utilisation over a 24-hour cycle, and a meaningful slice of the "busy" time is idle-but-reserved: notebooks holding memory overnight, jobs left running after people went home, and a batch pipeline that hogs two cards but touches them at maybe 20% intensity. In other words, a good fraction of the latency we experience is self-inflicted. If we implemented fair-share scheduling, automatic preemption of idle sessions, and moved the batch pipeline to off-peak windows, I'd expect effective capacity to rise by 30–40% without spending a dollar on hardware. That is the opportunity cost argument in its purest form: every dollar spent on a new node is a dollar not spent on the scheduling work that would make the new node unnecessary — and if we buy first, the pressure to do that unglamorous work evaporates. Nobody optimises a queue that is no longer painful.

There's also the reliability angle, and it cuts both ways. More nodes means more redundancy: a single failed card today takes out a meaningful share of our capacity, and our mean time to repair is measured in days because we have no spare parts and no vendor SLA worth the name. A second node would halve our exposure to any single failure. But more hardware also means more things to fail and a maintenance burden our two-person infra rotation genuinely cannot absorb. Meanwhile, the utilisation improvements — better scheduling, checkpointing so jobs can be preempted and resumed, monitoring that actually tells us what's running — are the same investments that make us more resilient. A fleet that can drain and reschedule work gracefully survives hardware failures better than a bigger fleet that can't.

Then there's reversibility, which I think is the decisive factor. Hardware is a commitment with a half-life. It depreciates, it consumes power and rack space, and if our workload shifts — say we move fine-tuning to a hosted API for the models where latency tolerance is high — we can't return a GPU. Scheduling and tooling work, by contrast, is almost entirely reversible and, more importantly, portable: it makes whatever hardware we own, now or later, more productive. If we do the software work and still find ourselves queueing at 80% utilisation, that is a *clean signal* of genuine demand, and we can buy with confidence. If we buy now, we will never get that signal, because we'll have papered over the question.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. My 30–40% estimate is a judgement call, not a measurement; our telemetry is too coarse to say precisely how much capacity is trapped in idle reservations. It's possible the scheduling work yields only 15%, and we end up buying hardware a quarter later, having spent six weeks of engineering time along the way. I think that's an acceptable cost — six weeks of one engineer's time is cheap insurance against a five-figure capital commitment made on vibes — but it's a real cost and we should name it. There's also a scenario where the team grows or we take on a training project with hard deadlines, in which case latency stops being an annoyance and becomes a contractual risk, and buying becomes correct quickly.

So my recommendation: spend the next six weeks on utilisation — scheduler, preemption, telemetry, off-peak batching — with a pre-agreed trigger that if p95 queue latency still exceeds 30 minutes at sustained utilisation above 75%, we approve the hardware purchase without further debate. That sequencing gets us the information we need, keeps the option open, and avoids paying twice for capacity we may already own.

Happy to argue about the trigger threshold on Friday.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure working group
**Re:** Recommendation on our inference capacity plan for the next two quarters

**Status: For discussion, with a recommendation**

We've reached the point where our local GPU fleet is running hot. Peak-hour utilisation on the primary cluster has been sitting above 85% for three consecutive weeks, batch queues are backing up during business hours, and two teams have independently asked when they'll get guaranteed capacity. The obvious question on the table is whether we spend roughly $180K on two additional nodes or invest the next quarter in squeezing more out of what we already own. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because the framing matters more than the arithmetic.

The case for buying is straightforward and shouldn't be dismissed. Latency is a product feature for us. Our interactive workloads — the code-assist service and the internal search reranking — have p99 latency targets that we're currently missing during the afternoon peak, and no amount of clever scheduling fully fixes that when the hardware is genuinely saturated. Every millisecond of queueing shows up directly in colleague experience, and there's a real risk that teams start quietly routing around our infrastructure, which fragments everything and makes the utilisation problem worse, not better. Reliability is the other half of this: at 85%+ steady-state utilisation we have almost no headroom for a node failure. When one of the four machines goes down for maintenance or a driver issue, we're not degraded, we're triaging. That's not a sustainable operating posture for infrastructure that a growing fraction of the company depends on.

But the case for improving utilisation first is stronger than it might appear, and it's worth being honest about why. Our own telemetry suggests the picture is muddier than the headline number. A meaningful share of our GPU-hours — I'd estimate 20 to 30%, though I want to flag that this is a rough estimate based on sampled logs, not a careful audit — goes to batch jobs, experimental runs, and development workloads that are not latency-sensitive at all. Those jobs can move. Right-sizing model serving (we're running several models at batch sizes and precision levels chosen in a hurry last year), consolidating the long tail of small deployments onto shared multi-tenant endpoints, and time-shifting batch work into the overnight window could plausibly free up the equivalent of one node's worth of capacity. That's $90K of hardware we don't have to buy, depreciate, power, and cool — and, just as importantly, $90K we don't spend before we know we need it.

The opportunity-cost argument cuts both ways, and I want to name it explicitly. Time spent on scheduling work, quantisation experiments, and queue tuning is senior-engineer time that isn't building product. If the team spends six weeks on utilisation work and we still need the hardware, we've delayed the purchase by six weeks and spent real salary cost getting there. That's a genuine risk. But the reverse risk is larger in my view: hardware bought to absorb waste gets locked in for three to five years. Once the purchase is made, the waste becomes invisible — nobody ever goes back to ask whether the second cluster was necessary. Utilisation work, by contrast, is highly reversible. If we spend three weeks on it and conclude the gains are illusory, we've lost three weeks and gained a much better empirical basis for the purchase request. If we buy hardware first and the gains were available, we've stranded capital and can't easily un-buy the machines.

There's also a timing consideration. GPU pricing and availability have been volatile, and our vendor quote is valid through the end of next quarter. Buying later carries some risk of worse pricing, but also the possibility of better options as the market shifts. I don't think we should bet the plan on that either way.

**My recommendation:** run a focused, time-boxed utilisation effort — four weeks, two engineers, with a hard checkpoint — while pre-approving the hardware purchase contingent on its outcome. If we can demonstrably move the latency-sensitive workloads below 70% peak utilisation, we defer the buy by a quarter and re-evaluate with real data. If we can't, we order the nodes immediately with the vendor quote intact, and the utilisation work still pays for itself in operating cost.

The honest uncertainty here is that our utilisation data is noisier than we'd like, and my 20–30% waste estimate could be off by half in either direction. That's precisely why the plan should be structured to learn quickly rather than to commit early. I'd rather spend four weeks finding out than $180K.

Happy to discuss at Thursday's sync.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Friday planning session

---

We've reached the point in the quarter where the queue for our inference cluster is long enough that people are asking, with some frustration, whether we should just buy more hardware. I want to lay out my thinking before we meet, because I believe the answer is more nuanced than the queue length suggests, and because the decision we make now will shape our cost structure for at least the next two years.

Let me start with the case for buying, because it's the emotionally intuitive one. Our p95 latency on the shared cluster has crept from 400ms to nearly a second during peak hours, and two of our product teams have shipped features whose user experience visibly degrades as a result. New GPUs would make that problem disappear overnight. The hardware itself is cheaper than it was a year ago, and the procurement path is well-trodden. If we order in the next two weeks, we could have capacity online before the next release cycle.

But that framing hides most of the real question. When I looked at the utilisation data, our fleet averages 38% GPU utilisation across the day, with peaks above 85% for roughly three hours and long troughs overnight and on weekends. We do not, in aggregate, have a capacity problem. We have a scheduling and fragmentation problem. Batch jobs from the training side sit idle during the day; inference capacity sits idle at night; and because teams have grown accustomed to reserving nodes rather than sharing them, we routinely have expensive silicon doing nothing while someone else waits in line. Buying more hardware in this state would be like adding lanes to a road whose traffic lights are misconfigured — it works, but it's the most expensive possible fix.

The utilisation path is not free, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. Introducing a proper scheduler with preemption and priority classes means engineering time — realistically, one person for six to eight weeks — and it means difficult conversations, because sharing means someone's overnight batch job can be evicted, and someone's interactive workload can no longer assume a node is theirs. There will be a transition period where reliability feels worse before it feels better. Latency for low-priority work may actually increase. These are real costs, paid in goodwill as much as in engineering hours.

Still, compare the two paths on their merits. Buying four more nodes costs roughly £180k up front, plus power, cooling, and the operational burden of a larger fleet — and, crucially, it locks in that spend. Hardware depreciates fast, our workload mix is shifting toward models we haven't fully characterised yet, and if the mix changes again, sunk capital is the least reversible thing we own. The utilisation work, by contrast, costs a fraction of that, and nearly every piece of it is reversible: scheduler policies can be relaxed, priority classes rewritten, batch windows rescheduled. If we improve utilisation and still hit a wall in six months, we will have lost little, learned a great deal about our true demand curve, and can buy with far better information. If we buy now and the demand spike turns out to be a two-team artefact, we've spent £180k to avoid an uncomfortable conversation.

There's also the opportunity cost of our own attention. The same engineer who would build the scheduler could instead ship the caching layer that would cut inference load by perhaps 20% on its own. I'd rather not treat hardware and software as substitutes when they're complements — better caching makes whatever capacity we have go further, and a scheduler makes the caching gains available to everyone rather than to whichever team owns the node.

My recommendation, then: we commit to the utilisation work for one quarter, with a concrete target — p95 latency under 500ms at peak and fleet utilisation above 60% — and a pre-agreed trigger. If we miss that target by the end of Q3, we buy the hardware, no further debate, and the quarter's work still leaves us with a scheduler that makes the new fleet cheaper to run. That structure lets us act decisively without pretending we know things we don't. The honest uncertainty here is about demand, not engineering: I'm confident we can raise utilisation; I'm not confident how much headroom that buys us. The trigger handles that.

I'd like a decision in Monday's session. Come with objections — the plan is deliberately falsifiable, and I'd rather stress-test it now than in month three.
